newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil Cerj sold to Enersis-led group.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil Cerj sold to Enersis-led group.

text.p: Rio de Janeiro state's privatization program got off to a good start with Cerj, the first of the state's companies to be privatized, achieving a lofty price of 605.3 million reais ($587.7 million), analysts said.

Matty Vengerik at CS First Boston in New York said the auction price, which was 30.3 percent above the minimum asking price of 464.7 million reais ($451.2 million), was "the best price ever paid" for an electricity company in Latin America with more than 500,000 customers.
"This company has 1.2 million customers, and for that size, it's a great price," said Vengerik, an analyst who specializes in the electricity sectors of emerging markets.

A 70.2 percent stake in Companhia de Eletricidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (Cerj) was snatched up by a consortium led (behind the scenes) by Chilean power investment firm Enersis SA, the largest private power holding company in Latin America valued at more than $4 billion.
The remaining 7.8 percent of the state's 78 percent stake in Cerj is being sold to Cerj employees.
The consortium included two Panamanian firms, one of which is wholly-owned by Enersis and the other by power distribution company Chilectra, which in turn is 75 percent owned by Enersis.
The one owned by Enersis bought a 30.6 percent stake and the one by Chilectra a 29.4 percent holding.
Also in the consortium were Spanish electricity company Endesa Desarollo SA and Portuguese power firm Electricidade de Portugal (EDP), which bought 10 percent and 30 percent respectively.

Chilectra President Marcos Zylberberg said $500 million would be invested in Cerj over the next five years, with 60 percent of the amount in the first two years. This compares with investments in Cerj of 57 million reais ($55.3 million) in the past two years.

Cerj supplies 75 percent of Rio de Janeiro state's territory with electricity and accounts for 20 percent of consumption with energy sales of 5,400 gigawatt hours in 1995 and 4,100 gigawatt hours in the first nine months of this year.
Vengerik was optimistic about Cerj's future performance because its new owners were all foreign "industry players" who would expose the company to different methods of operation and new standards.

"I have seen these particular owners in different forms and they know how to do it. They turn their companies around," he said. "I think Cerj has a very large upside. Under the right management, it can be a very successful company."
Cerj posted a loss of 62 million reais ($60.2 million) in 1995 and a loss of 126 million reais ($122.3 million) in the first nine months of this year.

Zylberberg said the consortium was interested in developing the Brazilian electricity sector, and was not looking for short-term gains, but for maximum returns on its investment in 15 to 30 years time.
He said he expected electricity demand in Brazil to grow an annual six to seven percent on a "permanent" basis in coming years.

"As the Brazilian market normalizes its economic situation and as the privatization programs advance, electricity demand will increase substantially because per capita income in the country will grow," Zylberberg said.

Vengerik said the main task for Cerj's new owners will be to resolve the company's energy losses, which come to 28.5 percent of production, compared with a Brazilian average of 12 percent and a 9 percent average in the United States.
-- Simona de Logu, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151
